lede: A regular season good enough to win most years: 14–5, 4.9 categories a week, fourth seed. Then a 2–7 quarter-final loss to Brighton, a 9–0 win over the Foxes, and a sixth-place finish after a final week in which only 38 starting slots were set. Ats won the regular season two ways — a draft that supplied 58% of the production, and one of the best waiver records in the league.
profile: Blocks were the anchor: won in 20 of 22 matchups, second in the league with 570. Around them, a team that was quietly fourth in five categories — points, threes, rebounds, steals and turnovers. That is rare breadth. The one real hole is assists: 12th of 14, 5–16–1. It is a punt nobody chose — the drafted core is bigs and wings, with no lead ball-handler. FG% at 10th, despite the bigs, is the wings' volume shooting.
ledger: 108 of 198 categories. The one-category weeks went 5–1 — close games were won. Brighton is the story. The Infirmary played them three times and lost all three — 4–5 in week 10, 3–6 in week 18, 2–7 in the playoffs. A blocks-and-counting team has little to fall back on against another team of bigs that wins FG% every week. That matchup, not the 14–5 record, decided the season.
draft: The middle of the board carried it. Bam Adebayo at $28 banked 2,270 and Trey Murphy III at $24 banked 2,213, both more than the $38 Chet Holmgren (1,879, kept all year). The value picks were wings at $9: Toumani Camara (1,665, 185 per dollar) and Jaden McDaniels (1,604). The cheap misses were quick and small. Bennedict Mathurin ($8), Zaccharie Risacher ($5), Egor Demin ($1) and Christian Braun ($9) were all gone by day 25. Mathurin went on to 1,384 for someone else. Zach LaVine and Norman Powell ($28 between them) left on day 34.
production: 42% acquired after the draft — below most of the league. The biggest addition came by trade: Anthony Edwards arrived on day 35 and banked 1,941 in 46 games, 42 a game, the best rate on the roster. Kevin Porter Jr. added 1,072, and P.J. Washington, claimed on day 25, added 1,058.
trades: Only two trades all season, and both were good business. Day 34 sent LaVine and Powell to Ben's Need Some VC. The incoming side could not be recovered from the data, but Edwards joined the lineup the next day. Day 49 sold Franz Wagner for Kyshawn George, +484: Wagner played ten more games all year, while George banked 697 here. That is selling a player at exactly the right moment.
wire: 1.56 net production a day per swap — third in the league — with a 62% hit rate. 67 claims won from 330 attempts, all $100 of FAAB spent, and never more than $10 on a single player. That is efficient, patient wire work. The best moves came in the same week: P.J. Washington on day 25 (+11.9) and Peyton Watson on day 26 (+13.8). The one slip followed a day later, dropping Watson for Josh Okogie (−10.2).
bench: Twenty wasted player-days, 560 production — second most in the league. Three of the six biggest came on the final day of the season: Gary Trent Jr. 48, Toumani Camara 37 and Devin Carter 35, all benched on day 160. Across the regular season the lineup was well managed.
last: The fifth-place game, and it looks like the season had already ended for this roster. 38 starting slots set against 50, and one of nine on the final day. The result was 3–6, with points 507 to 810 and assists 87 to 190. It cost a place in the final standings and nothing more. But it is on the page.
closing: A strong manager's season. The draft found value in the $9–$28 range, the wire was among the league's best, and two trades were both well timed. A 14–5 record is not an accident. It ended against the one opponent built to beat it. The fix is in the category profile: assists at 5–16–1 is a free category handed to every opponent, every week. One genuine playmaker would have made the Brighton matchup — and every close week — a different calculation. Keep the wire approach exactly as it is. It was the best thing about this team.
